extracted.intended_audience: readers of Whitman's Specimen Days; general literary readers and aspiring writers (creative non‑fiction/memoir audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing literary memoir/creative nonfiction and character reportage — rendering hospitals, crowds, biography fragments, and personal reminiscence with vividness and moral/psychological insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gratitude as source of highest poetry/art
rubrics_metrics.description: "Gratitude, anyhow, has never been made half enough of by the moralists; it is indispensable to a complete character... I am not sure but it is the source of the highest poetry--as in parts of the Bible. Ruskin, indeed, makes the central source of all great art to be praise (gratitude) to the Almighty for life, and the universe with its objects and play of action."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make gratitude (deep appreciation/praise for life and the world) a central emotional/ethical element in character and in the work; Whitman judges the 'giving thanks part' of life and writing as 'essentially the best item' and says gratitude 'rounds the whole emotional nature.' Works that embody this appreciative trend attain higher poetic/artistic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer genuine individual memoranda/cases over bare statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: "a few genuine memoranda of such things--some cases jotted down '64, '65, and '66--made at the time and on the spot, with all the associations of those scenes and places brought back, will not only go directest to the right spot, but give a clearer and more actual sight of that period, than anything else."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting large events (war, social conditions), use close, on‑the‑spot anecdotes and specific cases rather than relying solely on aggregate figures; vivid particulars convey truth and emotional reality more effectively than statistics alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let subjects speak; be a listener and ask suggestive questions
rubrics_metrics.description: "I get along, very sociably, with any of them--as I let them do all the talking; only now and then I have a long confab, or ask a suggestive question or two. I talk now and then with them, and learn much that is interesting and significant."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In reporting and gathering material from people/crowds, adopt a listening posture: allow them to talk freely and interject only occasional, suggestive questions. This elicits natural speech, authentic detail, and surprising insights useful for literary reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center portraits on inner truth / the self's inherent relations
rubrics_metrics.description: "E.H. gives the service of pointing to the fountain of all naked theology, all religion, all worship, all the truth to which you are possibly eligible--namely in _yourself_ and your inherent relations. Others talk of Bibles, saints, churches... E.H. to the religion inside of man's very own nature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying a person (biography or character sketch), emphasize their inner life and inherent relations rather than external dogma or formal trappings; bring forward personal, inward sources of belief and feeling as the locus of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be dominated by mannered phraseology; get to the main need
rubrics_metrics.description: "One must not be dominated by the man's almost absurd saturation in cut and dried biblical phraseology, and in ways, talk, and standard... the canting and sermonizing soon exhale away to any auditor that realizes what E.H. is for and after. The main need he drove home to the soul..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting mannered, clichéd, or rhetorical flourishes obscure the subject's essential truths. Prize substance over cant: stylistic affectations should not bury the core concerns or moral thrust of the portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete sensory detail to render scenes vividly
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples in the hospital scenes: "the convulsive spasms and working of muscles, mouth, and throat... two good women nurses... the doctor comes in and gives him a little chloroform... a white bandage is bound around and under the jaw... the broad white sheet is thrown over everything."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ immediate, tactile, visual, and auditory details (specific actions, physical symptoms, objects, gestures) to create vivid, emotionally affecting scenes. Whitman's close sensory specifics (smells, touches, motions) show how to make readers 'see' and 'feel' events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize subjects within broader historical and social background
rubrics_metrics.description: "While the foremost actors and events...were crowding each other on the world's stage...through all these whiles, I say...a curious, quiet yet busy life centred in a little country village... About this life, this Personality--neither soldier, nor scientist, nor littérateur--I propose to occupy a few minutes..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate individual lives and local scenes against the sweep of contemporary history and culture to highlight contrasts and illuminate significance. Providing lists of contemporaries, events, and social texture gives perspective and amplifies the subject's meaning.
